preamble: Fortition of the palatal lateral [ʎ] to the voiced palatal stop [ɟ], with the lateral approximant closing completely at the palatal place. The clearest case is Sicilian and the neighbouring southern Calabrian dialects, where the geminate palatal lateral from Latin -LJ- (preserved as [ʎʎ] in Italian figlio, olio) appears as geminate [ɟɟ], spelled -gghi-: figghiu 'son', ogghiu 'oil'. Some Sicilian varieties keep -gli- forms (figliu), showing the lateral stage the stop developed from. The Spanish example formerly filed here was a chain: yeísmo merged /ʎ/ into /ʝ/, and [ɟ] is a positional allophone of /ʝ/, so it is not a direct ʎ > ɟ shift.

examples.note: The geminate palatal lateral from Latin -LJ- surfaces as a geminate voiced palatal stop.

examples.from: Latin oleum, cf. Italian olio, oglio
examples.note: Same development; central-southern Sicilian varieties (Agrigento, Caltanissetta, Enna) further weaken -ggh- to the fricative [ʝ].
